Title: Document 5
Subtitle: John Hay, United States Secretary of State, The Second Open Door Note, July 3, 1900
Content: To the Representatives of the United States at Berlin, London, Paris, Rome, St. Petersburg, and Tokyo Washington, `text(July 3, 1900)`

In this critical posture of affairs in China it is deemed appropriate to define the attitude of the United States as far as present circumstances permit this to be done. We adhere to the policy . . . of peace with the Chinese nation, of furtherance of lawful commerce, and of protection of lives and property of our citizens by all means guaranteed under extraterritorial treaty rights and by the law of nations. . . . We regard the condition at Pekin[g] as one of virtual anarchy. . . . The purpose of the President is . . . to act concurrently with the other powers; `text(first)`, in opening up communication with Pekin[g] and rescuing the American officials, missionaries, and other Americans who are in danger; `text(secondly)`, in affording all possible protection everywhere in China to American life and property; `text(thirdly)`, in guarding and protecting all legitimate American interests; and `text(fourthly)`, in aiding to prevent a spread of the disorders to the other provinces of the Empire and a recurrence of such disasters. . . . The policy of the Government of the United States is to seek a solution which may bring about permanent safety and peace to China, preserve Chinese territorial and administrative entity, protect all rights guaranteed to friendly powers by treaty and international law, and safeguard for the world the principle of equal and impartial trade with all parts of the Chinese Empire.
